c.tagline: A honey-colored stone city cascading down a hillside over the Mesopotamian plain
langs: Syriac (Aramaic, among the local Christian community)

card: Widely accepted at hotels and mid-range restaurants; the old bazaar's small shops often prefer cash.
rides: dolmuş minibuses within the old city and to Midyat

taxi.fare: Roughly ₺30-50 flag fall plus metered per-km rate
taxi.fareNote: Metered fares are standard; a fixed rate is common for day trips to Midyat or Deyrulzafaran Monastery

religion: Syriac Orthodox Christianity (a historic minority with several active monasteries and churches in and around Mardin)
walk: The old city's stepped, terraced stone streets are extremely walkable (and steep — expect a lot of stairs), with sweeping views over the Mesopotamian plain from nearly every turn; Deyrulzafaran and Midyat require a taxi or dolmuş.

safety.safety: Generally safe for solo travelers; Mardin is a well-established tourist destination, though as with the wider southeastern Turkey region, travelers should check current travel advisories given the area's proximity to the Syrian border
safety.crime: Violent crime against tourists is rare in the city itself; standard awareness of the regional political situation is advisable before planning a visit

hood_landmark.Old City (Eski Mardin): Kasımiye Madrasa and the honey-stone terraced streets
hood_landmark.Cumhuriyet Meydanı Area: Mardin's central square and clock tower
hood_landmark.Şar / Savurkapı: Şahtana Cistern and old city gate
hood_landmark.Yeni Mardin (New Mardin): Modern residential and commercial expansion below the old city

avoid.reason: Southeast near the Syria border — heightened security risk; check advisories before travel

hood_desc: The UNESCO-nominated historic core, a maze of honey-colored stone houses and madrasas cascading down the hillside — the essential base for exploring Mardin on foot.
The old city's civic heart, with the main square, clock tower, and the busiest concentration of shops and restaurants.
A quieter residential stretch of the old city near the historic Savur Gate, with fewer crowds and traditional courtyard houses.
The hillside district southeast of town holding the active Deyrulzafaran Syriac Orthodox Monastery, a working religious community since the 5th century.
The modern lower town where most locals now live and shop, offering a practical, non-touristy contrast to the historic hill above.

water.note: Tap water is chlorinated but locals drink bottled — do the same.

transit.sys: Dolmuş (shared minibus) network within the old city and to Midyat
transit.map: Dolmuş depart from the lower town near Cumhuriyet Meydanı
transit.note: The old city's stepped streets are best explored entirely on foot; a taxi is needed for Deyrulzafaran and Midyat day trips

transport.air: Mardin Airport (MQM), about 20 km away, has direct domestic flights from Istanbul and Ankara
transport.train: No passenger rail service to Mardin
transport.bus: Regional and long-distance coaches connect Mardin to Diyarbakır, Şanlıurfa, and other southeastern Turkish cities
transport.ferry: None — Mardin is inland on the Mesopotamian plateau with no ferry service
transport.car: Self-driving is useful for reaching Midyat, Dara, and Deyrulzafaran independently; roads are generally good

airport.name: Mardin Airport
airport.distance: ~20 km (25-30 min) from the old city
airport.transport: Taxi or pre-booked hotel transfer; roughly $15-25

net.m: Good 4G coverage in Mardin's old and new city; can weaken in outlying villages
net.w: Free wifi standard in hotels and cafes
net.fwn: Free wifi widely available in hotels and cafes
net.ap: A Turkcell or Vodafone tourist SIM or eSIM is recommended

tip.r: 10% is standard at restaurants where service isn't already included
